name: Squaric acid dibutyl ester

lead: Squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE) is a chemical that dermatologists apply to the scalp to provoke a mild allergic reaction, a method called contact immunotherapy. The aim is hair regrowth in people with alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy or complete hair loss, so it is used to restore scalp hair.

It is one of three contact sensitizers used in this way, alongside DNCB and diphencyprone (DPCP). Reviews report regrowth in a portion of patients, with outcomes varying between studies, and network meta-analyses rank it below DPCP and oral therapies in efficacy comparisons.

paras: In clinics, patients are first sensitized and then treated at intervals with dilute solutions applied to patches of scalp, with the reaction level adjusted by the clinician. Regrowth, when it occurs, is assessed over months. It is also used for resistant warts and has been trialled for recurrent cold sores.

Itching, redness, eczema-like rashes, blistering and swollen lymph nodes are the common local effects; vitiligo and erythema multiforme-like reactions are rare. Handling solutions can sensitize staff, so it is prepared and applied under supervision.

Local allergic reaction alters immune activity around follicles
angle.text: It is a clinic-based option for people with extensive alopecia areata who want scalp hair back. Results differ between individuals and studies.

lead: Squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE) is a topical contact sensitizer used as immunotherapy for alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of nonscarring hair loss. It is applied to the scalp to induce a controlled allergic dermatitis that, in some patients, is followed by hair regrowth.[1][2]

Topical immunotherapy for skin disease has been used since the 1970s, mainly for extensive alopecia areata and resistant viral warts. Three universal sensitizers have been used: DNCB, SADBE and DPCP, with DPCP considered by one review to have practical advantages.[2][3]

Evidence includes a 1985 controlled half-scalp trial in 17 patients that reported only minimal terminal hair growth in three patients and adverse effects,[4] a meta-analysis of contact immunotherapy outcomes,[5] and Cochrane and network meta-analyses comparing treatments.[1][6] Wikipedia also lists SADBE use for warts.[7]

paras: Contact immunotherapy with SADBE or DPCP is described in a meta-analysis as a preferred treatment for severe alopecia areata, though definitions of regrowth vary widely between studies.[5]
Topical immunotherapy has also been used for resistant warts.[2][7] A phase 2 randomized study examined a single dose of SADBE to reduce recurrent herpes labialis outbreaks.[8]

Local blistering and eczematous eruptions are the most common risks of topical immunotherapy; vitiligo and erythema multiforme-like reactions are rare. Medical, nursing and pharmacy staff can be sensitized, so solutions are handled carefully.[2] The 1985 trial reported adverse effects in most patients, leading to early withdrawal of two.[4]

The treatment is thought to work by altering the immune environment around hair follicles through a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to the sensitizer; reviews describe it as treating conditions thought to arise from an altered immune state.[2][9]

A Cochrane network meta-analysis (2023) evaluated treatments for alopecia areata including contact immunotherapy.[1] A 2024 network meta-analysis ranked oral dexamethasone, DPCP, ritlecitinib and baricitinib above SADBE in efficacy, with SADBE above placebo.[6] A 1985 controlled trial found minimal regrowth in 3 of 17 patients,[4] and later open studies and retrospective evaluations describe outcomes and factors influencing response.[10][11]
